question: You have a big serve and a big forehand. What's the single most productive pattern to build your service games around?
option_a: Serve big and wait to see what comes back
option_b: Serve to a spot that forces a predictable return into your forehand, then end the point with the forehand — the serve-plus-one
option_c: Go for an ace on every first serve
why_right: When you own a big serve and a big forehand, the highest-value pattern is to make them work together. A serve targeted to force a weak, predictable return into your forehand zone gives you a known ball to attack — you're not reacting, you're executing a rehearsed one-two. Waiting passively wastes the serve's advantage, and going for aces only invites double faults. The serve-plus-one forehand is the most repeatable way to win cheap, fast points on serve.
pro_insight: Andy Roddick's service games were built on the serve-plus-one forehand as much as on the serve itself. The serve was designed to elicit a return he could run around or step into with the forehand, ending the point on the next ball. The two weapons were one pattern, and that pattern made his serve games extraordinarily hard to break.
common_pitfall: Hitting a big serve but having no plan for the return, then reacting to it instead of attacking a known ball.
action_tip: Pick a serve location that forces the return into your forehand, then commit to ending the point with it — rehearse serve-plus-one as one pattern.
share_prompt: Big serve, big forehand — do you connect them?

question: It's a big point on your serve. You have a dominant first serve. What's usually the smarter target?
option_a: The opponent's strongest side, to prove you can
option_b: A spot you can hit with confidence and that exploits the opponent's weaker return — placement and reliability over showing off
option_c: Always down the T for the ace
option_d: A safe spin serve to just get it in
why_right: Big points reward reliability and leverage, not bravado. The smart target is a location you can execute under pressure and that attacks the opponent's weaker return wing or their least comfortable position. Always going down the T makes you predictable on the points that matter most; serving to their strength for its own sake is ego, not strategy; and a tentative spin serve invites a free attack. Pick a confident target that exploits a known weakness.
pro_insight: Andy Roddick's serve was a genuine weapon on big points precisely because he combined velocity with smart targeting, mixing locations so returners could not sit on a pattern. On the biggest points he served to spots he trusted that also pressured the returner's weaker side — leverage, not just speed, won those points.
common_pitfall: Becoming predictable on big points by always serving the same spot, or serving tentatively just to get it in.
action_tip: On big serving points, choose a target you trust that also attacks the opponent's weaker return — leverage over predictability.
share_prompt: Big point serve — show off, or exploit?

question: A ball lands in the middle of the court and you have time. You have a dominant forehand. What's often the strongest play?
option_a: Take it with whatever wing is closest
option_b: Run around it to hit the forehand, taking control of the rally with your stronger weapon while staying aware of the open court you expose
option_c: Always hit the backhand to stay balanced
why_right: A central ball with time is an invitation to impose your best shot. Running around the backhand to hit a dominant forehand lets you dictate with your strongest weapon and often end the point or force a weak reply. The trade-off is the open court you expose by moving across, so the shot has to be good enough to prevent an easy reply behind you. Taking it with the nearest wing wastes the chance to use your weapon; the calculated move is to run around and attack, aware of the recovery you owe.
pro_insight: Andy Roddick frequently ran around his backhand to unleash the forehand, his clear weapon, when a ball gave him time and central position. The decision was a deliberate trade: expose some court to impose the bigger shot. When the forehand was strong enough to force a weak reply, the exposed court never came into play.
common_pitfall: Running around the backhand on a poor ball or without recovering, leaving the open court exposed for an easy counter.
action_tip: On a central ball with time, run around to hit your forehand weapon — but make it strong enough to cover the court you expose.
share_prompt: Central ball — nearest wing, or run around to your weapon?

question: You're a big server but you've just been broken and feel the pressure mounting. What's the disciplined way to steady your service games?
option_a: Serve even bigger to make a statement
option_b: Trust your highest-percentage first serve and your serve-plus-one pattern — rely on the routine that holds, not on raising the risk
option_c: Start spinning in safe serves to avoid double faults
option_d: Change your service motion to find rhythm
why_right: Pressure tempts a big server toward extremes — either swinging harder and risking double faults, or babying serves in and inviting attack. Both raise the chance of a loose game. The steadying move is to trust the reliable first-serve target and the plus-one pattern that wins your routine points, keeping the risk where it normally is. The serve holds because the process holds; changing the motion or the risk level mid-match usually makes things worse.
pro_insight: Andy Roddick relied on a repeatable serve and a clear plus-one pattern to hold serve under pressure, rather than chasing bigger serves when the moment tightened. The discipline was trusting the process that worked all match instead of forcing the issue. Steadiness, not escalation, protected his service games.
common_pitfall: Reacting to pressure by serving harder or, conversely, spinning in safe serves — both increase the chance of a loose game.
action_tip: Under serving pressure, trust your reliable first serve and plus-one pattern — keep the risk normal, don't escalate or shrink it.
share_prompt: Just got broken — serve bigger, or trust the process?

question: You're playing on a fast, low-bouncing court that rewards a first-strike game. What pattern should dominate your tactics?
option_b: Shorten points deliberately — serve big, return aggressively, and look to end points within the first few shots before long rallies develop
option_c: Grind from the baseline and wait for errors
option_d: Use heavy topspin to push opponents back
why_right: A fast, low court rewards the player who strikes first because the surface gives less time to defend and the low bounce makes heavy topspin less effective. The tactic is to shorten points: a big serve, an aggressive return, and an intent to finish within the first few shots before the opponent can establish a defensive rally. Grinding or relying on topspin fights the surface; first-strike tennis works with it. The court itself is telling you to take time away.
pro_insight: Andy Roddick's first-strike game was especially potent on fast, low-bouncing courts where his serve and forehand could end points quickly. He used the surface to compress points, striking early rather than letting rallies extend. The game style matched the conditions — the fast court amplified the weapons.
common_pitfall: Playing long, patient rallies on a fast court that rewards striking first, surrendering the surface's advantage.
action_tip: On fast, low courts, shorten points with a big serve and aggressive return — aim to finish in the first few shots.
share_prompt: Fast court — grind, or strike first?

question: You're facing an opponent who is simply playing at a higher level today. What's the competitor's response that gives you the best chance?
option_a: Accept it's not your day and coast
option_b: Make them earn every point, hold your serve games tightly, and stay present so that if their level dips even slightly, you're right there to pounce
option_c: Take wild risks to try to shift momentum fast
option_d: Slow the match down with long breaks
why_right: When an opponent is genuinely better on the day, the way to stay in the match is to remove all free points, protect your serve, and keep the pressure on so that any dip in their level finds you ready. Levels fluctuate; a tight, present competitor capitalizes the moment the other player wavers. Coasting concedes the match outright, and wild risks just speed the loss. Competing means staying close enough that a small swing in their level becomes your opening.
pro_insight: Andy Roddick was respected as a fierce competitor who made opponents earn everything, even on days he was outplayed. By holding serve tightly and refusing to give free points, he stayed within range so that any wobble in the opponent's level became a chance. The competitiveness kept matches alive that lesser fight would have ended.
common_pitfall: Mentally conceding when an opponent is playing better, instead of staying close enough to exploit any dip in their level.
action_tip: When outplayed, give no free points and protect your serve — stay close so a small dip in their level becomes your opening.
share_prompt: Outgunned today — coast, or make them earn it?
